name: Speed Dial
description: Polycarp's phone book contains $$$n$$$ phone numbers, each of them is described by $$$s_i$$$ — the number itself and $$$m_i$$$ — the number of times Polycarp dials it in daily. Polycarp has just bought a brand new phone with an amazing speed dial feature! More precisely, $$$k$$$ buttons on it can have a number assigned to it (not necessary from the phone book). To enter some number Polycarp can press one of these $$$k$$$ buttons and then finish the number using usual digit buttons (entering a number with only digit buttons is also possible). Speed dial button can only be used when no digits are entered. No button can have its number reassigned. What is the minimal total number of digit number presses Polycarp can achieve after he assigns numbers to speed dial buttons and enters each of the numbers from his phone book the given number of times in an optimal way?
input_specification: The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 500$$$, $$$1 \le k \le 10$$$) — the amount of numbers in Polycarp's phone book and the number of speed dial buttons his new phone has. The $$$i$$$-th of the next $$$n$$$ lines contain a string $$$s_i$$$ and an integer $$$m_i$$$ $$$(1 \le m_i \le 500)$$$, where $$$s_i$$$ is a non-empty string of digits from $$$0$$$ to $$$9$$$ inclusive (the $$$i$$$-th number), and $$$m_i$$$ is the amount of times it will be dialed, respectively. It is guaranteed that the total length of all phone numbers will not exceed $$$500$$$.
output_specification: Print a single integer — the minimal total number of digit number presses Polycarp can achieve after he assigns numbers to speed dial buttons and enters each of the numbers from his phone book the given number of times in an optimal way.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1082F — Speed Dial [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
